opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it is that looking at representations only tells you part of the story. You can take a model, look at the activations at some layer, and find directions that correspond to concepts — this is the model thinking about "Texas," this is the model thinking about "rhyming." That's really useful, and a lot of interpretability work over the last few years, including sparse autoencoders, has been about getting cleaner versions of those representations. But a representation is a snapshot. It tells you *what* is there; it doesn't tell you *how* it got there or *what it does next*.

What we actually care about, in a lot of cases, is the computation. If the model says "Austin" when you ask for the capital of the state containing Dallas, you want to know: did it actually go Dallas → Texas → Austin internally, or did it just memorize a shortcut from "Dallas" and "capital" straight to "Austin"? You can't answer that by looking at one layer's features in isolation. You need to see how features at one point cause features at another point.

The problem is that the real computation in the model goes through MLPs that are dense and polysemantic — every neuron participates in tons of things — so if you try to trace causal paths through the original model, you get an uninterpretable mess. That's where transcoders come in. Instead of just reconstructing the activations at a layer like an SAE does, a transcoder is trained to take the input to an MLP and predict its output, but through a sparse, interpretable set of features. So you're essentially swapping out the MLP's computation with a replacement that does approximately the same thing but in terms of features you can actually read.

Once you do that across the model — and with cross-layer transcoders, where a feature can write to multiple downstream layers — you get what we call a replacement model. And in that replacement model, you can draw an attribution graph: this feature fed into that feature, which fed into the output. That's the step change. You go from "here's a list of concepts the model is representing" to "here's a circuit, here's the mechanism," and you can test it — intervene on the Texas feature, swap it for California, and see whether the answer changes to Sacramento.

Of course, the replacement isn't perfect. There's always some error between what the transcoder computes and what the real MLP computes, and we try to be really upfront about that — we track those error terms in the graphs, and part of the work is checking whether the mechanisms we find actually hold up when you intervene on the original model. But even with those caveats, it's what lets us start making claims about *how* the model reasons, rather than just *what* it's thinking about, and that's the jump I think really matters.

r001.rationale: It says a representation is a snapshot that shows what is present, but not how it got there or what it does next; tracing how features cause later features requires more than inspecting one layer.

r002.rationale: It explains that transcoders replace MLP computation with an approximately equivalent computation through sparse, interpretable features, enabling circuit tracing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that there are really two questions you can ask about a model. One is "what is it representing?" and the other is "what is it doing?" And for a long time, a lot of interpretability work was focused on the first one. You train a sparse autoencoder on the residual stream, you get these features, and you can look at a feature and say, okay, this fires on the Golden Gate Bridge, this fires on code with a bug in it, whatever. And that's genuinely useful. It tells you the model has a concept for this thing.

But it doesn't tell you how the model uses that concept. It's a snapshot. You see what's there at layer 15, you see what's there at layer 16, and you kind of have to squint and guess what happened in between. And the thing that happened in between is the computation. It's the MLPs. That's where the model is actually taking features and combining them and producing new ones.

So the idea with transcoders is, instead of just reconstructing the activations at a point, you train something that mimics what the MLP layer does. It takes the input to the layer and it predicts the output of the layer, but it does it through a sparse, interpretable bottleneck. And now you have a replacement for that piece of the model. You can literally swap it in. And when you do that, you get something really nice, which is that the features now have inputs and outputs that you can read off directly. You can say this feature reads from these upstream features and writes to these downstream features, and the weights between them are just linear, so you can trace it.

That's what lets you build circuits. That's what lets you go from "the model knows about Texas" to "the model saw Dallas, that activated a Texas feature, Texas combined with a 'capital of' feature, and that produced Austin." You get a mechanistic story instead of a list of concepts. And honestly, the cases where it was most compelling to me were the ones where the story was surprising. Where you'd have assumed the model did one thing and it turns out the circuit does something else, or does the right thing for a reason you wouldn't have predicted.

The other piece, which I think is underrated, is that replacing the computation gives you a validation criterion. If I claim I understand what this layer does, well, does my replacement actually reproduce the model's behavior? How much of the performance do I recover? That's a hard, measurable thing. With pure representation analysis, it's much easier to tell yourself a nice story and have no way of being wrong. So it's not just that transcoders give you more information, it's that they keep you honest about whether the information is actually right.

r001.rationale: The response says representation snapshots at successive layers do not show what happened between them, identifying the intervening computation as what representation inspection misses.

r002.rationale: It explains that transcoders mimic an MLP through a sparse, interpretable bottleneck, can replace that layer, and enable tracing circuits.

astra-6.text:
Well, inspecting representations tells you something about what information is available inside a model, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how the model uses that information. You might find a feature that corresponds to a particular concept, but that alone doesn’t explain how it contributes to the next prediction.

With transcoders, the idea is to approximate a piece of the model’s computation using sparse, interpretable features. Instead of just asking, “What’s represented here?” we can start asking, “Which features cause other features to activate, and how does that lead to the output?” That gives us a way to trace computational paths and test them with interventions.

The important caveat is that the transcoder is an approximation. We need to check how faithfully it reproduces the original computation. But if it does that well, we’ve moved from identifying concepts to building a testable explanation of what the model is doing.

r001.rationale: The response says that identifying represented information does not explain how the model uses it or how it contributes to the next prediction, conveying that inspecting representations alone does not reveal the intervening computation.

r002.rationale: It says transcoders approximate a piece of the computation with sparse, interpretable features, but does not clearly state that they replace the model’s computation.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking at representations can tell you what information is present in a model, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what the model is doing with that information. You might find a feature that corresponds to a concept, but that alone doesn’t explain how that concept affects the next prediction.

With transcoders, we try to approximate a piece of the model’s computation using a sparse set of interpretable features. That gives us a way to trace how features in one part of the model contribute to features downstream. We can start moving from “the model represents this concept” to “this concept contributes to this intermediate step, which contributes to this output.”

The important caveat is that the transcoder is an approximation. We have to check how faithfully it reproduces the original computation and test the connections we think we’ve found. But it gives us a much more concrete starting point for understanding mechanisms, rather than just identifying things the model knows.

r001.rationale: The response says representations can show what information is present but not what the model does with it or how it affects the next prediction.

r002.rationale: It describes using transcoders to approximate a piece of the model’s computation with a sparse set of interpretable features, which communicates replacing that computation with a sparse approximation.
